# Part A: Whitening and Autocovariance Matrices

## Overview

This report implements Part A of the assignment: the preprocessing and matrix
computations required by the time-series version of the ladle estimator of
Nordhausen and Virta (2018). The report has two parts.

- **Section 1** defines the generic functions: centering, whitening,
  autocovariance estimation, symmetrization, and the AMUSE / SOBI diagonalizers.
- **Section 2** applies these functions to the course data `timeseries.dat` and
  verifies the implementation numerically.

All computations are implemented directly in R. The only ready-made routines used are
`JADE::rjd()` for joint diagonalization (as permitted by the assignment) and
`JADE::SOBI()` for an independent verification step. The functions defined here
are written so that they can be re-applied inside a bootstrap loop in Part C,
where each bootstrap sample must be re-centered, re-whitened, and
re-diagonalized.

---

## 1. Generic functions

### 1.1 Conventions

The sample size is $T$ (called $n$ in the assignment) and the dimension is $p$.

**Input convention:** every function that takes data expects a
numeric $T \times p$ matrix whose rows are the time points, in time order, and
whose columns are the variables. This matters in Part C, where every bootstrap
sample is again a $T \times p$ matrix: a transposed input would give a wrong
result without any error message. The following conventions are used
consistently.

- **Centering.** Column-wise subtraction of the sample mean:
  $$\bar{x} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} x_t, \qquad \tilde{x}_t = x_t - \bar{x}.$$

- **Scaling.** No additional marginal standardization (each column is not divided by its standard deviation first). Whitening uses the full sample
  covariance matrix, not only the column standard deviations, so it removes both
  the differences in scale and the contemporaneous correlation between columns.
  All scaling is absorbed into the whitening step. The whitening matrix is the
  symmetric inverse square root
  $$\hat{\Sigma}^{-1/2} = V D^{-1/2} V^\top,$$
  computed from the eigendecomposition $\hat{\Sigma} = V D V^\top$ of the
  sample covariance.

- **Lagging.** For a lag $\tau \ge 1$, the pairs $(x_t, x_{t+\tau})$, with
  $t = 1, \dots, T-\tau$, are used. No circular wrap-around in Part A.

- **Normalization.** The $1/T$ normalization is used throughout for the
  sample covariance and the autocovariance matrices:
  $$\hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \tilde{x}_t \tilde{x}_t^{\top}, \qquad \hat{\Sigma}_\tau = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T-\tau} \hat{x}_t^{st} \hat{x}_{t+\tau}^{st\top}.$$
  Here $\hat{x}_t^{st}$ denotes the *whitened* series, so the autocovariance
  is estimated on the whitened data. The $1/T$ normalization is the same
  convention as R's `acf(..., type = "covariance", demean = FALSE)`.

- **Symmetrization.** Under the model, $\Sigma_\tau$ is symmetric. The
  finite-sample estimate $\hat{\Sigma}_\tau$ is in general not symmetric, and
  its antisymmetric part is purely sampling noise. That part is removed:
  $$\tilde{\Sigma}_\tau = \frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{\Sigma}_\tau + \hat{\Sigma}_\tau^{\top}\right).$$
  Under the model, symmetrization removes sampling noise and does not remove
  signal.

- **Definition of $\Lambda$ and ordering.** Let $\tilde{\Sigma}_\tau$ be the
  symmetrized autocovariance matrix of the whitened series. The vector `Lambda`
  returned by these functions contains the diagonal elements of the matrix
  $\Lambda$ in the paper, that is, the values $\lambda_j^2$:

  - AMUSE (one lag $\tau$):
    $\lambda_j^2 = \left(u_j^\top \tilde{\Sigma}_\tau u_j\right)^2$.
  - SOBI (lag set $\mathcal{T}$):
    $\lambda_j^2 = \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} \left(v_j^\top \tilde{\Sigma}_\tau v_j\right)^2$.

  Here $u_j$ and $v_j$ are the columns of the estimated orthogonal matrix that
  belong to $\lambda_j^2$. In both cases the columns are ordered so that
  $\lambda_0^2 \ge \lambda_1^2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_{p-1}^2$. The paper indexes
  these values from $0$ to $p-1$, so `Lambda[k + 1]` in R is $\lambda_k^2$. Part C
  uses the same sorted `Lambda` and the same column order. In the theory the
  orthogonal matrix is called $U$. In the code it is called `U` for AMUSE and
  `V` for SOBI (`V` is the name used by `rjd()`).

### 1.2 Why whitening

In the second-order source separation (SOS) model

$$x_t = \mu + \Omega z_t, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(z_t) = I_p,$$

the covariance of $x_t$ is $\Sigma = \Omega\Omega^\top$, so the matrix
$\Sigma^{-1/2}\Omega$ is orthogonal. The whitened series is therefore

$$x_t^{st} = \Sigma^{-1/2}(x_t - \mu) = U z_t, \qquad U^\top U = I_p.$$

This has three consequences.

1. The unknown mixing matrix $\Omega$ reduces to an **orthogonal** matrix $U$.
2. The lag-$\tau$ autocovariance becomes
   $$\Sigma_\tau = U \, D_\tau \, U^\top, \qquad D_\tau = \operatorname{Cov}(z_t, z_{t+\tau}),$$
   If the component processes are mutually independent (assumptions (A1) and
   (A2) of Nordhausen and Virta, 2018), or at least uncorrelated across
   components at every lag, then $D_\tau$ is diagonal. The condition
   $\operatorname{Cov}(z_t) = I_p$ alone is not enough, because it only describes
   the components at the same time point. The diagonal form of $D_\tau$ is the
   condition that lets all the whitened lagged autocovariance matrices share the
   same diagonalizing matrix $U$. So a single lag can be diagonalized by
   `eigen()` (AMUSE), and a set of lags can be jointly diagonalized by an
   orthogonal matrix (SOBI).
3. Whitening removes scale and contemporaneous correlation; what is left in
   $\tilde{\Sigma}_\tau$ is the serial dependence that distinguishes signal
   components from white noise.

### 1.3 Functions

```{r functions}
center_series <- function(X) {
  # Subtract the column means
  mu_hat <- colMeans(X)
  Xc <- sweep(X, 2, mu_hat, FUN = "-")
  list(mu = mu_hat, Xc = Xc)
}

whiten_series <- function(Xc) {
  Tn <- nrow(Xc)
  p <- ncol(Xc)

  # Sample covariance (1/T) and its eigendecomposition, which must not be singular
  S <- crossprod(Xc) / Tn
  eig <- eigen(S, symmetric = TRUE)
  stopifnot(min(eig$values) > 1e-10 * max(eig$values))

  # Symmetric inverse square root and whitened data
  D_inv_sqrt <- diag(1 / sqrt(eig$values), nrow = p)
  S_inv_sq <- eig$vectors %*% D_inv_sqrt %*% t(eig$vectors)

  Xw <- Xc %*% S_inv_sq

  list(S = S, eig = eig, S_inv_sq = S_inv_sq, Xw = Xw)
}

# Lag-tau autocovariance of the whitened series: (1/T) * sum_t x_t x_{t+tau}'
autocov_raw <- function(Xw, tau) {
  # The lag must be valid
  stopifnot(tau >= 1, tau < nrow(Xw))
  Tn <- nrow(Xw)
  # Pairs (x_t, x_{t+tau}) for t = 1, ..., T - tau
  A <- Xw[1:(Tn - tau), , drop = FALSE]
  B <- Xw[(1 + tau):Tn, , drop = FALSE]
  crossprod(A, B) / Tn
}

# Remove the antisymmetric part
symmetrize <- function(M) {
  0.5 * (M + t(M))
}

# AMUSE: Lambda_j = (u_j' Sigma_tau u_j)^2 for ONE lag, sorted decreasingly
amuse_fit <- function(Sigma_tau_sym) {
  # The eigenvalues are u_j' Sigma_tau u_j
  eig <- eigen(Sigma_tau_sym, symmetric = TRUE)
  # Sort by lambda^2, not by the signed eigenvalue
  ord <- order(eig$values^2, decreasing = TRUE)
  list(
    U = eig$vectors[, ord, drop = FALSE],
    diag_vals = eig$values[ord],
    Lambda = eig$values[ord]^2
  )
}

sobi_fit <- function(X, lags = 1:12) {
  # Center, whiten and compute the symmetrized autocovariances at all lags
  cen <- center_series(X)
  wht <- whiten_series(cen$Xc)
  Xw <- wht$Xw
  p <- ncol(Xw)

  S <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(p, p, length(lags)))
  for (k in seq_along(lags)) {
    S[, , k] <- symmetrize(autocov_raw(Xw, lags[k]))
  }

  # Joint diagonalization
  V <- rjd(S, maxiter = 1000)$V

  # SOBI: Lambda_j = sum over lags of (v_j' Sigma_tau v_j)^2, then sorted decreasingly
  Lambda_raw <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(seq_along(lags), function(k) {
    diag(t(V) %*% S[, , k] %*% V)^2
  }))
  ord <- order(Lambda_raw, decreasing = TRUE)

  list(V = V[, ord, drop = FALSE], Lambda = Lambda_raw[ord], Xw = Xw, S = S,
       W = wht$S_inv_sq, mu = cen$mu)
}
```

---

## 2. Application to `timeseries.dat`

### 2.1 Data

```{r load-data}
ts_data <- as.matrix(read.table("timeseries.dat", header = FALSE))

cat("Dimension of the data (T x p):", dim(ts_data))
# Any missing values?
anyNA(ts_data)
```

The data have $T = 1000$ time points and $p = 10$ variables, so the input
convention of Section 1.1 holds (rows are time points and $T > p$). There are no
missing values.

### 2.2 Centering and whitening

```{r data-whiten}
# Center and whiten the data
cen <- center_series(ts_data)
mu_hat <- cen$mu
Xc <- cen$Xc

wht <- whiten_series(Xc)
S <- wht$S
Xw <- wht$Xw

cat("Column means after centering (should be approximately zero):")
print(colMeans(Xc))

cat("Eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix:")
print(wht$eig$values)
```

The column means after centering are zero up to rounding error. All eigenvalues
of the sample covariance matrix are positive (the smallest is about $1.0$), so
the inverse square root $\hat{\Sigma}^{-1/2}$ exists.

### 2.3 Numerical verification of whitening

The whitened sample covariance should be close to $I_p$:

$$\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \hat{x}_t^{st} \hat{x}_t^{st\top} \approx I_p.$$

Because we use the $1/T$ normalization, the check is against $I_p$. Had we
used R's `cov()` (which divides by $T-1$), the result would be
$\frac{T-1}{T} I_p \approx 0.999 I_p$, not $I_p$.

```{r data-verify}
# The whitened covariance should be the identity
S_white <- crossprod(Xw) / nrow(Xw)
err_F <- sqrt(sum((S_white - diag(ncol(Xw)))^2))
off_max <- max(abs(S_white - diag(ncol(Xw))))

cat("Frobenius distance ||S_white - I||_F =", signif(err_F, 4))
cat("Max absolute deviation from I =", signif(off_max, 4))
```

Both quantities are at machine precision, confirming the whitening has the
intended effect on the sample covariance matrix.

### 2.4 Autocovariance matrices

The autocovariance matrices of the whitened series are estimated at lags $1$ to
$12$ (the SOBI lag set used in Nordhausen and Virta, 2018) and symmetrized as
described in Section 1.1. The matrix at lag $1$ is used by AMUSE.
`sobi_fit()` recomputes all twelve matrices from the raw data, so that it can
be applied to bootstrap samples in Part C.

```{r data-autocov}
# Symmetrized autocovariance matrices at lags 1 to 12
lags <- 1:12
p <- ncol(Xw)

Sigma_sym_list <- lapply(lags, function(tau) {
  symmetrize(autocov_raw(Xw, tau))
})
```

### 2.5 Independent check of the autocovariances

The matrices are compared with R’s multivariate
`acf(..., type = "covariance", demean = FALSE)`, which computes the same $1/T$
sums of lagged products, including the cross terms between different columns.
Only the symmetrized matrices are used later, so both sides are symmetrized
before the comparison. This also means that the check does not depend on the
order of the two indices in the array returned by `acf()`.

```{r check-acov}
# Compare with acf(); both sides are symmetrized
a <- acf(Xw, lag.max = 12, type = "covariance",
         plot = FALSE, demean = FALSE)$acf

diffs <- sapply(lags, function(k) {
  max(abs(Sigma_sym_list[[k]] - symmetrize(a[k + 1, , ])))
})

cat("Max absolute difference versus acf() over all lags and entries:",
    signif(max(diffs), 4))
```

The difference is zero up to rounding error, so the autocovariance matrices
agree with R's own computation.

### 2.6 AMUSE (two-matrix / eigenvalue case)

AMUSE uses a single lag $\tau$ and finds an orthogonal matrix $U_\tau$ that
diagonalizes $\tilde{\Sigma}_\tau$:

$$U_\tau^\top \tilde{\Sigma}_\tau U_\tau = \text{diagonal}, \qquad \Lambda = \operatorname{diag}\left(U_\tau^\top \tilde{\Sigma}_\tau U_\tau\right)^2.$$

The columns of $U_\tau$ are reordered so that the corresponding $\Lambda$
values are decreasing. `amuse_res$Lambda` contains
$(\lambda_0^2, \dots, \lambda_{p-1}^2)$ as defined in Section 1.1. The lag is
$\tau = 1$.

```{r data-amuse}
# AMUSE at lag 1
tau_amuse <- 1
amuse_res <- amuse_fit(Sigma_sym_list[[which(lags == tau_amuse)]])

cat("AMUSE at lag tau =", tau_amuse)
cat("Lambda (decreasing):")
print(round(amuse_res$Lambda, 4))
```

### 2.7 SOBI (joint diagonalization via `JADE::rjd()`)

SOBI uses the lag set $\mathcal{T} = \{1, \dots, 12\}$ and jointly diagonalizes
$\tilde{\Sigma}_{\tau_1}, \dots, \tilde{\Sigma}_{\tau_K}$ by an orthogonal
matrix $U_{\mathcal{T}}$:

$$\Lambda = \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} \operatorname{diag}\left(U_{\mathcal{T}}^\top \tilde{\Sigma}_\tau U_{\mathcal{T}}\right)^2.$$

We use the function `sobi_fit()` defined in Section 1.3, which will also be
used in Part C for each bootstrap sample.

```{r data-sobi}
# SOBI with lags 1 to 12
sob <- sobi_fit(ts_data, lags = 1:12)
V <- sob$V

cat("SOBI Lambda (decreasing):")
print(round(sob$Lambda, 4))

cat("Orthogonality error ||V'V - I||_max =",
    signif(max(abs(crossprod(V) - diag(ncol(V)))), 4))
```

`sob$Lambda` contains $(\lambda_0^2, \dots, \lambda_{p-1}^2)$ as defined in
Section 1.1, so Part C can use it directly. The orthogonality error is at
machine precision, so $V$ is orthogonal.

As an independent check, we compare our components with those of the
ready-made `JADE::SOBI()`. This function is used only for this check. Because
the sign and the order of components are not identifiable, we compare them by
absolute correlation. For each of our components we report the best match and
the second-best match among the `JADE::SOBI()` components.

```{r data-sobi-check}
# Compare with JADE::SOBI, up to sign and order
ref <- JADE::SOBI(ts_data, k = 12)
C <- abs(cor(sob$Xw %*% V, ref$S))

best <- apply(C, 1, max)
second <- apply(C, 1, function(r) sort(r, decreasing = TRUE)[2])

cat("Smallest best-match correlation:", signif(min(best), 4))
cat("Largest second-best correlation:", signif(max(second), 4))
```

Each of our components has one match with absolute correlation close to $1$,
and all other correlations are close to $0$. Our solution and `JADE::SOBI()`
therefore produce the same components up to sign and order.

---

## 3. Summary of Part A

- **Conventions.** Column centering; no additional scaling; positive lags only;
  $1/T$ normalization (same as R's `acf(type = "covariance", demean = FALSE)`);
  symmetrization of the sample autocovariance matrices.
- **Whitening.** The series is whitened by the symmetric inverse square root
  $\hat{\Sigma}^{-1/2}$. Numerical verification shows the whitened sample
  covariance is at machine precision equal to $I_p$.
- **Autocovariances.** Estimated at lags $1$ to $12$ with $1/T$ normalization
  and no wrap-around. The antisymmetric part of the raw estimates is sampling
  noise and is removed by symmetrization. The symmetrized estimates agree with
  `acf()` to machine precision.
- **AMUSE.** One lag, base R `eigen()`, giving
  $\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(U_\tau^\top \tilde{\Sigma}_\tau U_\tau)^2$,
  ordered decreasingly.
- **SOBI.** Lags $1$ to $12$, joint diagonalization via `JADE::rjd()`, giving
  $\Lambda = \sum_\tau \operatorname{diag}(U_{\mathcal{T}}^\top \tilde{\Sigma}_\tau U_{\mathcal{T}})^2$,
  ordered decreasingly. Orthogonality of $V$ is at machine precision.
- **Verification.** An independent check with `JADE::SOBI()` confirms our SOBI
  solution agrees with the reference implementation up to sign and order.

The functions `center_series()`, `whiten_series()`, `autocov_raw()`,
`symmetrize()`, `amuse_fit()`, and `sobi_fit()` defined in Section 1.3 will be
reused in Part C, where each bootstrap sample must be re-centered, re-whitened,
and re-diagonalized. Part B only requires the original data matrix
`ts_data`.

---

# Part B: Bootstrap for Dependent Observations

## Overview

Part B implements two bootstrap methods for dependent multivariate
observations: the fixed-block bootstrap and the stationary bootstrap (SB) of
Politis and Romano (1994). 

Section 1 gives the methods and the implementation.
Section 2 shows how the methods behave on a strongly dependent
simulated series. Section 3 checks that the same functions work on the course
data as a general $T \times p$ matrix. Section 4 summarises.

Notation: $T$ is the number of time points, $p$ the dimension, and $X$ the
$T \times p$ data matrix with rows as time. The SB parameter is called
$p_{\mathrm{sb}}$ to avoid a clash with the dimension $p$.

---

## 1. Bootstrap functions

### 1.1 Why iid resampling is not appropriate

The iid bootstrap draws $X_1^*, \dots, X_T^*$ independently from
$\{X_1, \dots, X_T\}$ with replacement. The draws are independent, so the
resampled series has no serial dependence:
$\operatorname{Cov}^*(X_t^*, X_{t+\tau}^*) = 0$ for every $\tau \neq 0$,
whatever the dependence in the original series. For the ladle estimator this
is a problem, since it is built from the autocovariance matrices
$\Sigma_\tau$. An iid bootstrap sample has autocovariance matrices that only
reflect noise around zero, so the eigenvectors and the $f$ part of the ladle
would be computed from the wrong distribution.

Block resampling instead keeps consecutive observations together: the
dependence inside each block is preserved, and only the joins between blocks
break it. Since whole rows $X_t$ are resampled (Politis and Romano, 1994, Section 4.1),
the dependence between the $p$
components at the same time point, and between components at nearby lags, is
also kept.

### 1.2 Fixed-block bootstrap

Let $B$ be the block length and $h = \lceil T/B \rceil$. A bootstrap sample is
generated as follows (Nordhausen and Virta, 2018, Section 2).

1. Draw $h$ start points $s_1, \dots, s_h$ uniformly from $\{1, \dots, T-B+1\}$.
2. Block $j$ is $(X_{s_j}, \dots, X_{s_j+B-1})$.
3. The blocks are concatenated and the series is truncated to length $T$.

The tuning parameter is the block length $B$. Blocks do not wrap around, so
the first and last observations are covered by fewer blocks than the middle
ones, and the resampled series is not stationary. With $B = 1$ the method
reduces to the iid bootstrap.

### 1.3 Stationary bootstrap

The SB uses blocks with random lengths. Let $p_{\mathrm{sb}} \in (0, 1]$ be
the tuning parameter.

1. Draw a start point $s$ uniformly from $\{1, \dots, T\}$ and a block length
   $L$ with
   $$P(L = m) = (1 - p_{\mathrm{sb}})^{m-1} p_{\mathrm{sb}}, \qquad m = 1, 2, \dots$$
   This is the geometric distribution on $\{1, 2, \dots\}$; in R this is
   `rgeom(1, p_sb) + 1`.
2. The block is $(X_s, \dots, X_{s+L-1})$ with indices taken circularly:
   $X_{T+k} = X_k$.
3. Blocks are added until the series has length $T$; the last block is cut.

Since $E(L) = 1/p_{\mathrm{sb}}$, the *expected block length* is
$\ell = 1/p_{\mathrm{sb}}$, and a target $\ell$ is obtained with
$p_{\mathrm{sb}} = 1/\ell$. The tuning parameter is $p_{\mathrm{sb}}$, or
equivalently the expected length $\ell$. With $p_{\mathrm{sb}} = 1$ all blocks
have length one and the method reduces to the iid bootstrap. The circular
wrapping combined with the memoryless geometric lengths makes the SB
pseudo-series stationary conditional on the data (Politis and Romano, 1994,
Proposition 1).

### 1.4 Differences between the two methods

The SB uses random geometric block lengths with mean $1/p_{\mathrm{sb}}$ and
wraps the data around a circle, whereas the fixed-block bootstrap uses a
constant block length and does not wrap. As a consequence the SB pseudo-series
is conditionally stationary while the fixed-block pseudo-series is not. In the
SB, $\tau$ consecutive steps stay inside the same block with probability
$(1 - p_{\mathrm{sb}})^\tau$, so the dependence at lag $\tau$ decays
geometrically. In the fixed-block bootstrap, dependence is kept only for lags
shorter than $B$.

### 1.5 Implementation

All functions take a numeric $T \times p$ matrix with rows as time and resample
whole rows with a common index, so the dependence between components is kept.

```{r boot-functions}
# Index generators: each returns a vector of T row indices.
iid_index <- function(T) sample.int(T, T, replace = TRUE)

fixed_block_index <- function(T, B) {
  # h blocks of length B from random start points, cut to length T
  h <- ceiling(T / B)
  starts <- sample.int(T - B + 1, h, replace = TRUE)
  idx <- rep(starts, each = B) + rep(0:(B - 1), times = h)
  idx[1:T]
}

stationary_index <- function(T, p_sb) {
  # Geometric block lengths, enough to cover T
  lens <- integer(0)
  while (sum(lens) < T) {
    lens <- c(lens, rgeom(ceiling(2 * T * p_sb) + 10, p_sb) + 1)
  }
  # Random start points, circular indices
  lens <- lens[1:which(cumsum(lens) >= T)[1]]
  starts <- sample.int(T, length(lens), replace = TRUE)
  idx <- rep(starts, lens) + sequence(lens) - 1
  ((idx - 1) %% T + 1)[1:T]
}

# method is "iid", "fixed" (tuning = B) or "stationary" (tuning = p_sb).
boot_index <- function(T, method, tuning = NULL) {
  switch(method,
         iid = iid_index(T),
         fixed = fixed_block_index(T, tuning),
         stationary = stationary_index(T, tuning))
}

# List of M bootstrap samples, each a T x p matrix.
boot_samples <- function(X, M, method, tuning = NULL) {
  X <- as.matrix(X)
  lapply(seq_len(M), function(m)
    X[boot_index(nrow(X), method, tuning), , drop = FALSE])
}
```

`boot_samples()` returns $M$ matrices of size $T \times p$, which can be passed to the SOBI function of Part A to compute the ladle quantities.

---

## 2. Application to simulated data

The two methods are applied to a bivariate VAR(1) series with strong serial
dependence, so that the difference to iid resampling is clearly visible.

### 2.1 Data

```{r sim}
# Simulate a VAR(1) series, dropping a burn-in period
set.seed(123)
sim_var <- function(T, A, burn = 200) {
  p <- nrow(A)
  E <- matrix(rnorm((T + burn) * p), ncol = p)
  X <- matrix(0, T + burn, p)
  for (t in 2:(T + burn)) X[t, ] <- A %*% X[t - 1, ] + E[t, ]
  X[-(1:burn), ]
}

A <- matrix(c(0.8, 0.3, 0, 0.5), 2)
Xs <- sim_var(1000, A)

# ACF averaged over the components
avg_acf <- function(X, K = 30) {
  a <- acf(X, lag.max = K, plot = FALSE)$acf
  p <- ncol(X)
  sapply(0:K, function(k) mean(sapply(1:p, function(j) a[k + 1, j, j])))
}

# Average of avg_acf over the bootstrap samples
boot_avg_acf <- function(Zs, K = 30) {
  rowMeans(sapply(Zs, function(Z) avg_acf(Z, K)))
}
```

### 2.2 Index patterns

One realisation of the index vector is shown for each method with $T = 200$
and block length (or expected block length) $20$.

```{r index-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 2.3}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
set.seed(123)
plot(iid_index(200), pch = 16, cex = 0.4, main = "iid",
     xlab = "t*", ylab = "original index")
plot(fixed_block_index(200, 20), pch = 16, cex = 0.4, main = "fixed, B = 20",
     xlab = "t*", ylab = "")
plot(stationary_index(200, 1 / 20), pch = 16, cex = 0.4, main = "SB, mean length 20",
     xlab = "t*", ylab = "")
```

The iid panel shows scattered points with no structure. The fixed-block panel shows
straight segments of constant slope. The SB panel shows segments of varying
length, because the block lengths are geometric.

### 2.3 Autocorrelation of the resampled series

$M = 200$ bootstrap samples are drawn with $B = 20$ and $\ell = 20$
($p_{\mathrm{sb}} = 0.05$).

```{r acf-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3.5}
M <- 200
K <- 30
ell <- 20

a_orig <- avg_acf(Xs, K)
a_iid <- boot_avg_acf(boot_samples(Xs, M, "iid"), K)
a_fixed <- boot_avg_acf(boot_samples(Xs, M, "fixed", ell), K)
a_sb <- boot_avg_acf(boot_samples(Xs, M, "stationary", 1 / ell), K)

cols <- c("black", "gray", "blue", "orange")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(0:K, a_orig, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = cols[1],
     ylim = range(c(a_orig, a_iid, a_fixed, a_sb)),
     xlab = "lag", ylab = "average ACF over components")
lines(0:K, a_iid, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = cols[2])
lines(0:K, a_fixed, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = cols[3])
lines(0:K, a_sb, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = cols[4])
legend("topright",
       c("original", "iid", "fixed B = 20", "SB, mean 20"),
       col = cols, lty = 1, pch = 16, cex = 0.8, bty = "n")
```

The original series has strong serial dependence (lag-1 average ACF about
$0.7$). The iid bootstrap reduces this to essentially zero at every non-zero
lag. Both block methods are close to each other and lie slightly below the original ACF at the shorter lags (up to about lag 18), because the joins between consecutive blocks are usually not adjacent in the original series, so the local dependence is lost at those points. At larger lags all curves are close to zero.

### 2.4 Effect of the block length

For each $B$ and each $\ell = B$, $M = 200$ bootstrap samples are drawn. Two
summaries are reported: the average lag-1 autocorrelation over components, and
the bootstrap standard deviation of the sample mean (averaged over components).
The value $\ell = 1$ corresponds to the iid bootstrap.

```{r grid}
# Lag-1 ACF and SD of the sample mean over M bootstrap samples
grid_row <- function(X, method, tuning, M = 200) {
  Tn <- nrow(X); pp <- ncol(X)
  ids <- replicate(M, boot_index(Tn, method, tuning), simplify = FALSE)
  Zs <- lapply(ids, function(i) X[i, ])

  acf1_avg <- mean(sapply(Zs, function(Z) {
    a <- acf(Z, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf
    mean(sapply(1:pp, function(j) a[2, j, j]))
  }))

  means_mat <- sapply(Zs, colMeans)
  c(acf1 = acf1_avg,
    sd_mean = mean(apply(means_mat, 1, sd)))
}

ells <- c(1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200)
fx <- t(sapply(ells, function(b) grid_row(Xs, "fixed", b)))
sb <- t(sapply(ells, function(b) grid_row(Xs, "stationary", 1 / b)))

tab <- data.frame(
  ell = ells,
  acf1_fixed = fx[, 1], acf1_SB = sb[, 1],
  sd_fixed = fx[, 2], sd_SB = sb[, 2]
)
round(tab, 3)
cat("original lag-1 average ACF:", round(a_orig[2], 3))
```

At $\ell = 1$ both methods reduce to iid resampling, giving an ACF of about
$-0.004$ and an SD of the mean of about $0.05$. As $\ell$ increases, the
lag-1 ACF rises from the iid value towards the original value of $0.697$,
reaching about $0.69$ at $\ell = 200$. 

The bootstrap SD of the mean peaks at moderate block lengths: around $\ell = 50$ for the
fixed-block method ($0.132$) and $\ell = 20$ for the stationary bootstrap
($0.110$). For larger $\ell$ it decreases, dropping to about $0.08$ at
$\ell = 200$, where only a few blocks are drawn ($T/\ell = 5$). The two
methods give very similar ACF values at every $\ell$.

## 3. General check on the course data

The functions are applied to the course data `ts_data` (read in Part A) to
check that they work for a general $T \times p$ matrix with $p > 2$.

```{r course-load}
# A few bootstrap samples of the course data
Bd <- boot_samples(ts_data, 5, "stationary", 1 / 20)
c(n_samples = length(Bd), dim = dim(Bd[[1]]))

# Mean max deviation of the correlation matrix over N bootstrap replicates
set.seed(123)
N_corr <- 100
corr_dev <- function(method, tuning = NULL, N = N_corr) {
  mean(sapply(seq_len(N), function(n) {
    Z <- ts_data[boot_index(nrow(ts_data), method, tuning), , drop = FALSE]
    max(abs(cor(Z) - cor(ts_data)))
  }))
}

round(c(fixed      = corr_dev("fixed", 20),
        stationary = corr_dev("stationary", 1 / 20)), 3)
```
The average maximum deviation of the contemporaneous correlation matrix is 0.077 (fixed-block) and 0.075 (stationary), so the bootstrap samples keep the correlation of the course data.

## 4. Summary of Part B

- Ordinary iid resampling destroys the serial dependence and is not
  appropriate for time series. Block-based resampling preserves the local
  dependence by resampling consecutive runs of observations.
- The fixed-block bootstrap resamples blocks of length $B$. The SB uses
  geometric block lengths with mean $\ell = 1/p_{\mathrm{sb}}$ and wraps
  around, which makes it conditionally stationary. Both reduce to iid
  resampling when $B = 1$ or $p_{\mathrm{sb}} = 1$.
- On a strongly dependent VAR(1) series, the block methods preserved the
  average ACF (slightly below the original values), while iid resampling did
  not. The bootstrap standard
  deviation of the mean was largest at moderate block lengths.
- The functions run on the $1000 \times 10$ course data.

# Part C: The ladle quantities

Implement the quantities $f$ , $g$, and $\varphi$ used in the ladle estimator as defined in the paper.

Your report should explain what information is represented by the eigenvalue-based part and
by the bootstrap-variability part of the criterion, and how these quantities are combined to
estimate the dimension.

Check your implementation carefully on simulated data. Intermediate computational checks
should be described where they help establish that the implementation is correct.

## Answer:

The function $f_0(k)$ is defined for $k=1,\dots,p-1$ as $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n(1-|\text{det}(\hat{B}_k^T B_{k,j}^*)|)$, where $\hat{B}_k^T$ are the first $k$ columns of the joint diagonaliser computed from the original sample and $B_{k,j}^*$ are the first $k$ columns of the joint diagonaliser computed from the $j$th bootstrap sample, and $f_0(0)=0$. The function $f(k)$ is then extracted from $f_0(k)$ by normalising in the following way: $f(k)=f_0(k)/1+(\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}f_0(l))$.

The function $\varphi(k)$ is defined with the diagonal elements of $\Lambda$, $\lambda_0^2,\lambda_1^2,\dots,\lambda_{p-1}^2$. The diagonal elements are in a decreasing order. The (normalised) function $\varphi(k)=\lambda_k^2/(1+\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\lambda_l^2$.

After obtaining $f$ and $\varphi$, obtaining the ladle function $g$ is easy. The ladle function is defined as $g(k) = f(k) + \varphi(k)$. The ladle estimator for the dimension will be $\hat{q} = \argmin \{g(q)\}$.

In the ladle function $g$, the information represented by the bootstrap-variability is found in the normalised variance function $f$. This is quite obvious, because it is the only quantity in $g$ that contains components stemming from bootstrapping. The variance function $f_0$ is a way of finding out the average variance of the space, which is spanned by the first $k$ vectors. The information represented by the eigenvalues is found mainly in $\varphi$, but also in $f$. The function $\varphi$ is essentially a scree plot, which contains the eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix of the centred and whitened data calculated with either AMUSE or SOBI.


Here we define the function ladle, which computes the ladle quantities $f$, $\varphi$ and $g$.

```{r}
ladle <- function(data, j, method, tuning, fit) {
  # Calculate f
  k <- dim(data)[2] - 1
  B_star <- list(NA)
  sd_boot <- numeric(k+1)
  
  if(fit == "sobi") {B_hat <- sobi_fit(data)$V}
  if(fit == "amuse") {
    X <- data
    Xc <- center_series(X)$Xc
    Xw <- whiten_series(Xc)$Xw
    M <- autocov_raw(Xw, tau = 1)
    Sigma_tau_sym <- symmetrize(M)
    B_hat <- amuse_fit(Sigma_tau_sym)$U
  }
  
  Bd <- boot_samples(data, j, method, tuning)

  f_0 <- matrix(rep(0,(k+1)*j), nrow = j)
#  print(f_0) # For checking if the matrix has the right dimensions
  
  # Conditioning based on which method is specified to be used for joint diagonalisation
  if(fit == "sobi") {
    for (i in 1:j) {
      B_star[[i]] <- sobi_fit(Bd[[i]])$V
    }
  }
  
  if(fit == "amuse") {
    for (i in 1:j) {
      X <- Bd[[i]]
      Xc <- center_series(X)$Xc
      Xw <- whiten_series(Xc)$Xw
      M <- autocov_raw(Xw, tau = 1)
      Sigma_tau_sym <- symmetrize(M)
      B_star[[i]] <- amuse_fit(Sigma_tau_sym)$U
    }
  }
  # Loop that calculates the matrix, which will be used for f_0 
  for (m in 1:j) {
      B_star_j <- B_star[[m]] 
      for (i in 1:k) {
        f_0[m,i] <- (1-abs(det(crossprod(B_hat[,1:i], B_star_j[,1:i]))))
    }
  }

  f_0 <- cbind(f_0[,k+1], f_0[,1:k])
  
#  print(f_0) # For checking if the first column is 0
  
  f_0 <- colMeans(f_0) # Actual f_0
#  f <- c(f_0[k+1], f_0[1:k])
  f <- f_0/(1 + sum(f_0))
  
  # Calculate phi
  l <- dim(data)[2]
  phi <- numeric(l)
  
  # Conditioning based on which method is specified to be used for joint diagonalisation
  if(fit == "sobi") {
    Lambda <- sobi_fit(data)$Lambda
    for (i in 1:l) {
      phi[i] <- Lambda[i]/(1+sum(Lambda))
    }
  }
  
  if(fit == "amuse") {
    X <- data
    Xc <- center_series(X)$Xc
    Xw <- whiten_series(Xc)$Xw
    M <- autocov_raw(Xw, tau = 1)
    Sigma_tau_sym <- symmetrize(M)
    Lambda <- amuse_fit(Sigma_tau_sym)$Lambda
    for (i in 1:l) {
      phi[i] <- Lambda[i]/(1+sum(Lambda))
    }
  }
  
  # Calculate g
  g <- f + phi
  
  return(list(f = f, phi = phi, g = g))
}
```

# Part D: Simulation study
Use the simulation setting specified as Setting 1 in the paper to investigate the behaviour of
your implementation.

You are not required to reproduce every numerical result or figure in the paper. Instead,
reproduce the main qualitative behaviour of the estimator under Setting 1 and use the
simulation to demonstrate that your implementation works as intended.

Compare the fixed-block and stationary bootstrap approaches. Choose reasonable block-length
settings and justify the choices. Investigate whether the estimated dimension is sensitive to
the bootstrap method, block length, or sample size.

Your simulation study should contain enough independent repetitions to support the conclu-
sions, but computational effort should be used sensibly. Report Monte Carlo results in a way

## Answer:

"Throughout the simulations we considered model (1) with p = 10 and q = 5 where the five signal components are ARMA(0.6; (0, -0.4)), ARMA((0.4, 0.1, 0.3); (0.2, 0.4)), AR(0.4), MA(0.5, 0.3, 0.1,
0.2) and AR(0.1, 0.1, 0.3), all having Gaussian innovations. In Setting 1 the five noise components are all Gaussian white noise."

The simulation study will be done by using the same signal generation process as in Nordhausen & Virta, 2018. For process length, $T = 200, 500, 1000, 2000$ were considered. 10 bootstrap samples were used.

First we will define the functions that will be used to generate the signals.
```{r}
AR1 <- function(phi, n, burn = 200) {
  X <- numeric(n + burn)
  eps <- rnorm(n + burn)
  for (i in 2:(n + burn)) {
    X[i] <- phi * X[i-1] + eps[i]
  }
  X <- X[-(1:burn)]
  return(X)
}
```

Longer burn-in period, because there are more parameters for the more complicated models

```{r}
AR3 <- function(phi, n, burn = 500) {
  X <- numeric(n + burn)
  X[1:3] <- rnorm(3)
  eps <- rnorm(n + burn)
  for (i in 4:(n + burn)) {
    X[i] <- phi[1]*X[i-1] + phi[2]*X[i-2] + phi[3]*X[i-3] + eps[i]
  }
  X <- X[-(1:burn)]
  return(X)
}
```

```{r}
MA4 <- function(theta, n, burn = 500) {
  X <- numeric(n + burn)
  eps <- rnorm(n + burn)
  X[1:4] <- rnorm(4)
  for (i in 5:(n + burn)) {
    X[i] <- eps[i] + theta[1]*eps[i-1] + theta[2]*eps[i-2] + theta[3]*eps[i-3] + theta[4]*eps[i-4]
  }
  X <- X[-(1:burn)]
  return(X)
}
```

```{r}
ARMA12 <- function(phi, theta, n, burn = 500) {
  X <- numeric(n + burn)
  eps <- rnorm(n + burn)
  X[1:2] <- rnorm(2)
  for (i in 3:(n + burn)) {
    X[i] <- eps[i] + phi*X[i-1] + theta[1]*eps[i-1] + theta[2]*eps[i-2]
  }
  X <- X[-(1:burn)]
  return(X)
}
```

```{r}
ARMA32 <- function(phi, theta, n, burn = 500) {
  X <- numeric(n + burn)
  eps <- rnorm(n + burn)
  X[1:3] <- rnorm(3)
  for (i in 4:(n + burn)) {
    X[i] <- eps[i] + phi[1]*X[i-1] + phi[2]*X[i-2] + phi[3]*X[i-3] + theta[1]*eps[i-1] + theta[2]*eps[i-2]
  }
  X <- X[-(1:burn)]
  return(X)
}
```

min500_fixed_sobi_20 <- numeric(sims)


min1000_fixed_sobi_20 <- numeric(sims)


min2000_fixed_sobi_20 <- numeric(sims)


set.seed(107)
for (i in 1:sims) {
  ladle_estimates <- ladle(sim[1:200,], 10, "fixed", 20, "sobi")
  min200_fixed_sobi_20[i] <- which.min(ladle_estimates$g)
}
set.seed(106)
for (i in 1:sims) {
  ladle_estimates <- ladle(sim[1:500,], 10, "fixed", 20, "sobi")
  min500_fixed_sobi_20[i] <- which.min(ladle_estimates$g)
}
set.seed(107)
for (i in 1:sims) {
  ladle_estimates <- ladle(sim[1:1000,], 10, "fixed", 20, "sobi")
  min1000_fixed_sobi_20[i] <- which.min(ladle_estimates$g)
}
set.seed(108)
for (i in 1:sims) {
  ladle_estimates <- ladle(sim[1:2000,], 10, "fixed", 20, "sobi")
  min2000_fixed_sobi_20[i] <- which.min(ladle_estimates$g)
}

# Part E: Application to the course data

Apply the methods to the time-series data set provided for the assignment in Moodle.
Use both the fixed-block and stationary bootstrap versions of the ladle estimator. Select and
justify the block-length choices used in the final analysis.

Your analysis should include:

• the estimated signal dimension and the evidence supporting it;

• an appropriate visualization of the ladle criterion and its components;

• a comparison of the results obtained with the two bootstrap methods;

• a sensitivity analysis for the block-length choice;

• a discussion of what the results imply for the structure of the observed multivariate
time series.

If the two bootstrap approaches or different reasonable block lengths lead to different conclu-
sions, this should be investigated and discussed rather than hidden by reporting only one
result.

## Answer:

The previous part indicates that using SOBI for diagonalisation gives the most accurate results. For bigger block sizes there is almost no difference between fixed block bootstrap and stationary block bootstrap. The fixed block bootstrap method is faster, based on how long the simulations took.

```{r}
set.seed(456)
ts_ladle <- ladle(ts_data, 500, "fixed", 40, "sobi")
ts_ladle2 <- ladle(ts_data, 500, "fixed", 60, "sobi")
ts_ladle3 <- ladle(ts_data, 250, "stationary", 1/40, "sobi")
ts_ladle4 <- ladle(ts_data, 250, "stationary", 1/60, "sobi")
ts_ladle5 <- ladle(ts_data, 5, "fixed", 60, "sobi")
ts_ladle6 <- ladle(ts_data, 1000, "fixed", 60, "sobi")
```

```{r}
plot(ts_ladle$g, type = "l")
plot(ts_ladle2$g, type = "l")
plot(ts_ladle3$g, type = "l")
plot(ts_ladle4$g, type = "l")
plot(ts_ladle5$g, type = "l")
plot(ts_ladle6$g, type = "l")
```
